title: Devices: CPU, CUDA, and Tensor Placement
description: Every tensor lives on exactly one device — CPU or CUDA — and operations require all operands on the same one. Learn the canonical device-agnostic idiom that ports between machines.

sections.title: A tensor lives on exactly one device

data.markdown:
Every PyTorch tensor's storage lives in **exactly one place** — the host's CPU memory, a CUDA GPU's memory, or another accelerator (`mps` on Apple Silicon, `xpu`, …). Read it off any tensor with `t.device`:

```python
import torch

x = torch.randn(2, 3)                  # CPU is the default
print(x.device)                        # device(type='cpu')

if torch.cuda.is_available():
    y = torch.randn(2, 3, device='cuda')
    print(y.device)                    # device(type='cuda', index=0)
```

The rule that drives ~90% of device bugs in real PyTorch code is short:

> **All operands of an operation must live on the same device.**

Mix a CPU tensor and a CUDA tensor in one expression and PyTorch refuses:

```
RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device,
but found at least two devices, cuda:0 and cpu!
```

There is no implicit transfer. You decide where each tensor lives, and you keep them together.

*Device strings.* `'cpu'` is unambiguous. `'cuda'` is shorthand for `'cuda:0'` — the current default GPU; on a multi-GPU box `'cuda:1'` selects index 1. The host program runs on the CPU regardless: the GPU is a co-processor with its own separate memory.

sections.title: .to() returns a new tensor — bind the result

data.markdown:
The canonical move-and-cast operation is `Tensor.to(...)`. It is **not in place** — it returns a new tensor on the target device (or returns `self` unchanged if the source is already on that device with a matching dtype):

```python
x = torch.randn(2, 3)                  # CPU
x.to('cuda')                           # silently discarded — new tensor not bound!
x = x.to('cuda')                       # correct — rebind to capture the move
```

The same shape applies to the convenience aliases — `.cpu()`, `.cuda()`, `.float()`, `.double()` — they all return a new tensor. Forgetting the assignment is one of the most common device bugs in PyTorch code, and it fails *silently*: the old CPU tensor is still bound to `x`, and only later does an op crash when it expects `x` to be on the GPU.

A second subtlety: when source and target match exactly, `.to()` returns the original tensor (no copy). So calling `x = x.to(device)` repeatedly is cheap when nothing changes — useful when you write a function that doesn't know whether its input is already on the target device.

data.taskMarkdown:
Real PyTorch code rarely hard-codes `'cpu'` or `'cuda'`. It picks the best available device **once**, at the top of the script, then threads that `device` variable through every tensor and model construction. The same source then runs unchanged on a CPU-only laptop and a multi-GPU server.

Fill in the three blanks below — this exact idiom appears in nearly every official PyTorch tutorial.
data.template:
import torch

# Pick the best device once. On a CPU-only machine this falls back to 'cpu'.
device = 'cuda' if torch.{{cuda_check}} else 'cpu'

# Build a tensor on CPU, then move it to the chosen device.
# Remember: .to() returns a NEW tensor — always bind the result.
x = torch.randn(3, 4)
x = x.{{move_call}}

# Both operands of an op must live on the same device — pass it explicitly.
y = torch.zeros(3, 4, device={{device_arg}})

print((x + y).device)

slots.hint: The function on the torch.cuda submodule that returns True when a CUDA GPU is reachable. Don't forget the parentheses — it's a call, not a property.
The method that returns a new tensor on the target device. It takes the device as its argument.
Pass the same variable you computed two lines up — don't re-derive it.

hints.markdown: The `torch.cuda` submodule has a probe that returns `True` when a CUDA GPU is reachable: `torch.cuda.is_available()`. The `.to(...)` method takes the destination device and returns the moved tensor.

sections.title: Quick check: what's wrong with this line?

data.question: A colleague writes `x.to('cuda')` on a fresh line, then later sees `RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device` when `x` is added to a CUDA tensor. What is the bug?
options: `x.to('cuda')` only works when `x` is already a leaf tensor with `requires_grad=True`.
`x.to('cuda')` returns a new tensor on the GPU; the result was not bound back to `x`, so `x` is still on the CPU.
PyTorch silently transfers tensors between devices, so the error must come from something else.
`'cuda'` is not a valid argument to `.to()` — they should have written `.gpu()` instead.
data.explanation: `.to(...)` is **functional**, not in-place. It returns a new tensor on the target device (or `self` if no move is needed) and the colleague forgot to bind the result. The fix is one character: `x = x.to('cuda')`. PyTorch never moves tensors between devices implicitly — the runtime error you see later is exactly the safety net that catches this kind of mistake. (`.gpu()` does not exist; `.cuda()` is a valid alias for `.to('cuda')` but has the same bind-the-result rule.)

data.starterCode:
import torch

# Discover what devices this machine actually offers.
print('CUDA available :', torch.cuda.is_available())
print('Device count   :', torch.cuda.device_count() if torch.cuda.is_available() else 0)
print('Default dtype  :', torch.get_default_dtype())

device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
print('Chosen device  :', device)

x = torch.randn(2, 3)
print('x.device       :', x.device)

# The convenience aliases all return a NEW tensor — try forgetting the assignment
# and watch x.device stay on the CPU even though .cuda() ran without error.
# x.cuda()                         # discarded
# x = x.to(device)                 # the right shape

# A re-move to the same device is a no-op (returns self) — cheap to call defensively.
# x = x.to(device)
data.encouragement: Try toggling between `'cpu'` and `'cuda'` (when available) and printing `(x + y).device` after each move — feel where the rule "same device on both sides" actually bites.
